Human Agent

Agents: the full docs are one file at /llms-full.txt. This page as markdown: /agents.md.

pragma, for your agent

Everything an agent needs to build with pragma, in files it reads without a browser. Human: copy the prompt, paste it into your coding agent and say what to build.

The prompt

Replace the brackets with your app. The agent reads the docs, installs pragma, creates the app and runs pragma check --strict until it passes.

Read https://pragma.leonavas.com/llms-full.txt and create a pragma app that [describe your app]. Install pragma if missing, or validate the version with pragma -V and .pragma/version and run pragma self-update and pragma upgrade if outdated. Follow the AGENTS.md that pragma new writes into the app, and finish with pragma check --strict at zero errors and zero warnings.

Install and create

One Rust binary. On Linux and macOS, run the installer. On Windows, download the binary from GitHub Releases. On other platforms, build from source with Cargo. Node 22 or newer only runs .server.js files.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leonavas/pragma/main/install.sh | sh
pragma new my-app
cd my-app
pragma dev

Validate version and update

Validate the pragma version before you change code:

  • Run pragma -V to check the installed CLI version.
  • Compare that version with .pragma/version inside the app.
  • Run pragma self-update to update the CLI binary from GitHub Releases if the CLI is old.
  • Run pragma upgrade inside the app to update .pragma/ (runtime, docs, base.css, version) if .pragma/ is outdated.
pragma -V
cat .pragma/version
pragma self-update
pragma upgrade

Files for agents

Same content as the HTML pages, in markdown. No hidden text, nothing written only for agents.

  • /llms-full.txt: the app rules and every doc in one file. Start here.
  • /llms.txt: the index, in the llmstxt.org format.
  • /index.md: the landing page.
  • /agents.md: this page.

A request for / or /agents with Accept: text/markdown gets the markdown file instead of the HTML. One doc per file:

  • /docs/rules.md: the rules of every app (AGENTS.md). Read first.
  • /docs/structure.md: where each file goes, pragma.json.
  • /docs/syntax.md: HTML directives and blocks.
  • /docs/components.md: components, props, slots.
  • /docs/state.md: script, actions, derived values, stores.
  • /docs/routes.md: pages, router, head tags.
  • /docs/data.md: load, server actions, SSR.
  • /docs/overlays.md: modal, alert, dropdown.
  • /docs/forms.md: select, styled select, form values.
  • /docs/css.md: styles and theme.
  • /docs/classes.md: every utility class.
  • /docs/webmcp.md: forms as agent tools, markdown for agents.
  • /docs/packages.md: npm packages.
  • /docs/performance.md: defaults and the size report.
  • /docs/logs.md: OpenTelemetry logs.
  • /docs/cli.md: commands and check rules.

WebMCP tools on this site

This page and the landing page expose these tools to agents in the browser, as declarative WebMCP forms. Humans use the same forms. The landing page also has add_task (its demo to-do list), and /examples/data/demo/guestbook has sign_guestbook.

routes/examples/components/index.html:
A component is a file

routes/_components/counter/counter.html is the component <p-counter>. The pages in routes/ and its folders can use it. It has the same syntax as a page, but exactly one root element.

Each instance has its own state: two counters, two counts. A component in lib/components/counter/ is <c-counter> and works on every page.

Props: export let

export let sale = false declares a prop: a value that the page gives with an attribute, sale. The default decides the type, so sale="false" arrives as the boolean false. A missing attribute gives the default.

Object props: :prop="path"

An attribute is text. To give an object, bind it with a colon: :person="person". The component reads the object and does not change it.

Slots: content from the page

<slot> shows the children that the page puts in the tag. <slot name="actions"> shows only the children with slot="actions". The content of a <slot> shows when the page gives nothing.

Slot content belongs to the page

The page writes the slot content, so {$likes} and @click="like" read the page's script, not the panel's. The panel only decides where the content goes.

A component without a script

Without a script, a component still reads its attributes as $label and $star. The compiler resolves it when it builds the page, so it sends plain HTML and no JavaScript.

A component that uses itself

A component can use its own tag. Put it inside <for> or <if>, so it stops when the data ends. Here the data is in routes/index.js: a page script can be a .js file next to the page, instead of a <script>.

load() with a skeleton

routes/catalog.server.js runs on the server, next to the page routes/catalog.html. Its load function returns the data, and the page reads it as data.products. While load runs, page.loading is true, so the page shows a skeleton block.

  • A query change is a navigation, so load runs again.
  • A file named _name.server.js is a private helper. It never reaches the browser.

When load fails

error(503, 'message') from 'pragma/server' stops load with that status. The page gets it as page.error, so the <else-if page.error> branch shows.

ssr = true: data in the first HTML

With export const ssr = true, the server runs load and sends the page with its data in the HTML. There is no skeleton, and search engines see the data.

The server context: cookies and more

load and every action get one context object. cookies.get reads a cookie of the request and cookies.set adds it to the response. A cookie is httpOnly, sameSite: 'lax' and secure by default.

The context also has request, url, params, query, env (secrets and bindings), log, locals, setHeaders and waitUntil.

Writes go through server actions

A server action writes data. call('sign', input) runs actions.sign in the .server.js file and returns its result; the page assigns it to data. new FormData(event.target) reads the form fields.

Every form is also a tool for AI agents in the browser (WebMCP). toolname, tooldescription and toolparamdescription describe it, and event.respondWith gives the agent the result.

When an action fails

error(409, 'message') in an action makes call throw. The error has status, body (what the server sent) and message, so the page can react to each status.

Redirects: redirect()

redirect(303, url) from 'pragma/server' sends the browser to another page. After an action, the page navigates before call returns. In load, it replaces the current page, so Back skips it.

Middleware: before every request

routes/_middleware.server.js runs before every page, load, action and endpoint. It is the place for auth: it puts the user in locals for load and the actions, and redirects when a path needs a user. next() gives the response, which it can change.

An app has one middleware, so this site cannot run this one. The output is real, from a new app with this file.

curl -sI localhost:5197/account
HTTP/1.1 303 See Other
location: /login

curl -sI localhost:5197/
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-frame-options: DENY

Endpoints: a .server.js without a page

A .server.js with no .html next to it is an endpoint. It exports GET, POST and the other methods, and each returns a Response: a file, a stream, a webhook reply. A link with download opens it without the router.

Page data comes from load, and writes go through actions. Do not make /api endpoints for them.

Stream from an action: stream()

An action can return a Response with a ReadableStream. With content-type: application/x-ndjson, each line is one JSON value. stream('ask') gives each line as soon as the server writes it, in a for await loop.

Each input type gives its own value

:model keeps the type of the value. A number or range input gives a number, a checkbox gives true or false, and a group of radios gives the value of the checked one.

Each field has a label: a <label> around it, or a <legend> for a group.

Select: native first

A native <select> works with the keyboard, with screen readers and on phones. :model holds the value of the option, not its label. Style the box with utilities; do not change its appearance.

A styled list: c-select

When the list needs its own look, use <c-select>. It is in lib/components/select/ of every new app. It opens a dropdown and keeps a hidden native <select name> in sync, so new FormData(event.target) reads it like any field.

Every form is also a tool for agents, so it has a toolname and a tooldescription. WebMCP explains them.

Validation: browser rules, then yours

Native attributes come first: required, type="email", min, minlength. The browser stops the submit and shows its message, so @submit runs only with valid fields.

A rule between two fields goes in the submit function. It puts its message in state, in a role="alert" element.

Submit to a server action

Some rules need the server, for example a name that must be free. The action stops with error(409, message), and call throws: failure.message is the text for the form. The guestbook shows the success path.

routes/examples/layout/index.html:
A row: flex

flex puts the children in a row. items-center aligns them vertically, justify-between pushes them to the two ends and gap-4 keeps space between them.

A stack: flex-col and gap

flex-col puts the children in a column. gap-3 sets the space between them and p-4 the space inside the border. max-w-xs limits the card width, and w-full makes the button as wide as the card.

Columns: grid and col-span

grid-cols-3 makes three equal columns. A child takes one column, and col-span-2 makes it take two: here, a nav and a wider content area.

Responsive: sm:, md:, lg:

Breakpoints are mobile first: a class with no prefix applies on every screen, and sm:grid-cols-2 applies from 40rem up. lg: starts at 64rem. mx-auto w-full max-w-3xl centers the content and limits its width.

A sticky header in a scrolling list

h-48 overflow-auto gives the list a fixed height and its own scroll bar. sticky top-0 keeps each letter at the top while its names scroll under it. bg-surface hides the names below.

On top: relative and absolute

absolute top-0 right-0 places the dot at the top right of the nearest relative parent, out of the flow. z-10 keeps it above its siblings.

Logging from utils/

A plain module in utils/ imports the same client logger from .pragma/log.js. Its records join the same batches and trace.

import { log } from '../.pragma/log.js'

export function formatPrice(cents) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(cents)) {
    log.warn('price is not in cents', { 'price.value': cents })
  }
  return (cents / 100).toFixed(2)
}

Where the records go

Client batches go to the server at /_otel (up to 256 KB each), which forwards them with its own records. The standard OpenTelemetry variables configure it, so any OTLP/HTTP collector works.

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otel.example.com node dist/server/node.mjs

Never log passwords, tokens, cookies, emails or other personal data, and never log in loops or on each keystroke. console.* fails the check with js/console. On a static host there is no /_otel: the client stops sending after the first 404 or 405.

Dropdown

<c-dropdown> is a menu under its button. It closes on an outside click, Esc and @close.

Stacking, and close(id) from a script

An overlay can open another one. close('editor') from 'pragma' closes an overlay from a script.

Restyle and animate

A class on <c-modal> restyles it. To animate the close, style [data-leaving]: the runtime waits for the animation.

Install, list, import

Any package manager works: pragma reads package.json and node_modules/. A client import must be in dependencies. Check the platform first: Intl, fetch, crypto.randomUUID() and structuredClone cost nothing.

npm i valibot dayjs --ignore-scripts
grep -A6 dependencies package.json
  "dependencies": {
    "dayjs": "^1.11.23",
    "es-toolkit": "^1.53.2",
    "highlight.js": "^11.12.0",
    "valibot": "^1.5.0"
  }

Each package becomes one file, /assets/npm/<package>-<hash>.js, with a modulepreload on the pages that import it.

Named imports: only what you use ships

Import only the names you need. These four names ship 0.94 kB gzip of valibot, not the whole package.

Load a package on click with import()

When a package is needed only after a click, import it in a utils/ module, then await import() that module in the action. The package does not load with the page, and the module keeps its import open to tree shaking.

What common packages cost

Gzip size of the /assets/npm/ file for each import, from pragma build on the test app in core/cli/xtask/packages/app. For scale: the starter page ships 12.3 kB gzip of JS, runtime included. CommonJS (dayjs, lodash) ships whole.

Tree shaking, measured: highlight.js

The code on this site is colored by highlight.js. The package index pulls in all 193 languages; highlight.js/lib/core plus three grammars is 95% smaller. It runs in load on the server; the browser loads it only on the SEO page, with import().

Packages that fail the check

Real pragma check output. The error points at the import. UI frameworks are rejected because the runtime owns the DOM. Node built-ins run only in .server.js. TypeScript, JSX, .vue, .svelte and packages that import CSS fail with app/package.

Packages on the server

A .server.js file can import any package from package.json and Node built-ins (node:fs, node:crypto) without listing them. Server code is not bundled: Node resolves node_modules at run time.

WebAssembly on the server

A .server.js file can import a .wasm file. The import gives a compiled WebAssembly.Module on Node and on Workers. Here routes/_add.wasm exports one function, add.

pragma build copies the file to dist/server/ and adds the CompiledWasm rule to dist/server/wrangler.jsonc. Workers cannot compile WebAssembly from bytes, so give a package the imported module (Emscripten packages: instantiateWasm).

Workers modules and client imports

cloudflare:workers, cloudflare:sockets and the other cloudflare:* modules work in .server.js on Workers only. On Node (pragma dev, pragma serve) env from cloudflare:workers is the same env that load gets; any other export throws when it is used. Prefer the env that load and actions get. A file in routes/ is a page

routes/index.html is the page at /. routes/about.html is the page at /about. A folder adds a segment: routes/blog/index.html is /blog.

A page is a piece of HTML, with no <html> or <body>: the app adds them. <title> names the browser tab. A plain <a href> moves between pages, without a full reload. A URL with no file gets routes/_404.html, with status 404.

The root layout: routes/_layout.html

routes/_layout.html wraps every page: the header and the footer stay, and the page goes in <main data-page>, at <slot>. It has one <main data-page> with only the slot inside.

A layout has no <script>. It reads only shared, params and query, for example {shared.cart.count}. For behavior, put a component in it.

Params: [slug].html

routes/shop/[slug].html answers every URL of the form /shop/<anything>. The page reads that part of the URL as params.slug.

A layout for a folder

routes/shop/_layout.html wraps every page in routes/shop/ and its subfolders. The root layout wraps it in turn: root, then shop, then the page at the inner <slot>.

A folder layout has no <head> and no <main>: only its markup and one <slot>. A link to the current page gets aria-current="page", ready for CSS.

The query string: query

import { query } from 'pragma' gives the query string: ?tab=reviews is query.tab. A tab in the URL survives a reload and a shared link.

The current link for a query

aria-current is automatic only for a link without a query. For ?sort=price, bind :aria-current to a function that gives 'true' for the current link and false for the others. false removes the attribute.

Navigate from a script

navigate(url) opens a page from a script, like a click on a link. Use it after an action, for example after a save.

What the router does for free

  • Swaps only <main data-page> and the page's <title>, <meta> and <link>. Layouts stay mounted.
  • Prefetches a link on hover, on focus and when it scrolls into view.
  • Uses document.startViewTransition where the browser has it.
  • Scrolls to the top, restores the position on back and forward, follows #hash and moves focus to <main>.

Tags from server data

Use {data.x} in <title> and :content on <meta>. With export const ssr = true, the server fills the tags, so link previews see them.

Soft 404 and real 404

Change state in place

State is tracked deeply: items.push(…) updates the list on the page. There is no need to copy the array.

Derived values

A value computed from state is a function: const total = () => tickets * 12. The markup reads it as {$total}, with no call, and it follows each change. In the script, call it: total().

Async actions

An async function updates the page before each await and again after it.

mount() and its cleanup

A function named mount runs in the browser after the page shows. Start timers and listeners there. The function that it returns runs when the reader leaves the page: stop them there.

Animation: frame

import { frame } from 'pragma' gets a service of the runtime. frame(step) runs step in the next animation frame. To animate, step asks for the next frame until it is done.

Wrapped handlers

A const that holds a function is a handler too. So a function made by debounce, from the npm package es-toolkit, works in @input="saveLater".

Services from 'pragma'

All runtime services come from import { … } from 'pragma'. The next pages show each one:

  • shared: stores (Stores).
  • params, query, navigate: the URL (Routing).
  • data, page, call: server data and actions (Data).
  • open, close, confirm: overlays (Overlays).
  • log: logs (Logs).

Script mistakes that check catches

These four mistakes give no error in the browser, only a wrong or stale value. pragma check stops each one and names the fix.

Coming from state(ctx)

  • export const state = () => ({ count: 0 }) is now let count = 0.
  • export const actions is now top-level functions; ctx.scope.item is an argument: @click="remove(item)".
  • ctx.update(fn) is gone: assign the let. ctx.$.prop is export let prop.
  • ctx.data, ctx.call and ctx.log come from 'pragma'.

The old API fails check with js/legacy-api, and each message names the replacement.

Utilities and variants

The utility classes have the same names as in Tailwind v4. A variant such as hover: applies a class in one state. A class outside the list is a check error.

Tokens generate utilities

Each --color-<name> in lib/theme.css becomes a set of utilities: --color-accent gives bg-accent, text-accent and border-accent.

Custom classes and the cascade

A class used in many places, such as .btn, goes in @layer components in lib/theme.css. A utility beats a theme class, and the <style> of a component beats a utility.

Component CSS, scoped by the build

A <style> in a component applies only to that component. The build adds a scope to each selector.

Values from state: :--name

There is no style attribute. :--progress="$progress" puts a value in a CSS variable, and the CSS reads var(--progress).

Values that change every frame

For a value that changes each frame (pointer, scroll, drag), set it in frame and use it only in translate, scale, rotate or opacity. These properties do not compute the layout again.

Enter and leave motion

The root of an <if> or <for> item gets data-entering when it comes in and data-leaving when it goes. The element stays until its CSS animation ends. Without an animation, it goes at once.

Light and dark theme

dark: utilities apply inside data-theme="dark". The next example sets it for the whole page.

Theme toggle

theme() and setTheme() from .pragma/theme.js read and set the theme of the page. The choice stays for the next visit, and a first visit follows the system setting.

Script and text: {$name}

Each example on this page is routes/index.html, the home page of a new app. A <script> at the top of the page holds its values. A top-level let is state: a value that can change.

{$name} puts the value of name in the text. The $ says that the name comes from the script. Braces work in attribute strings too: title="Hi {$name}".

Events: @click

@click="add(1)" calls the function add of the script with the argument 1. The function assigns score, and the page shows the new value. No other step is necessary.

Without parentheses, @click="add" gives the function the DOM event. Any DOM event works: @input, @keydown, @submit.

Two-way binding: :model

:model="$name" keeps the field and name equal: typing changes name, and a new name changes the field. A checkbox gives a boolean, a number field a number.

Logic goes in a function

The HTML takes names, not code: {$name.toUpperCase()} is an error. Write a function in the script and use its name: {$loudName} calls loudName() on each render, so it always follows name.

Attributes: :attr

:disabled="$locked" sets the attribute from a value. true adds it and false removes it. This works for any attribute: :href, :title, :aria-expanded.

Class toggles: .class

.line-through="$done" adds the class line-through while done is true, and removes it when it is false.

:show hides, <if> creates

:show hides the element and keeps it in the page. <if $open> adds its content when open is true and removes it when it is false.

Conditions: <else-if> and <else>

After <if>, add <else-if> and <else>. One branch shows at a time. Each condition is a name: loading and failed are functions.

Lists: <for> and <empty>

<for task in $tasks key=task.id> repeats its element for each task. The key must be unique for each item. @click="remove(task)" gives the function the task of that row. <empty> shows when the list is empty.

A form is a tool

toolname and tooldescription on a <form> make it a tool. Each field with a name is a parameter, and toolparamdescription tells the agent what to type.

toolautosubmit lets the agent submit without a click. Use it only on safe forms, such as add or search. The handler reads the fields with FormData.

Reply to the agent

event.agentInvoked is true when an agent submits. event.respondWith(promise) gives the agent the result as JSON. Call it before any await.

Reply with errors too, so the agent can try again. A reply can also come from a server action: see the guestbook.

CSS while an agent fills the form

:tool-form-active matches the form while an agent fills it, and :tool-submit-active matches its submit button. The starter styles both; this component sets its own style.

    Install

    pragma is one Rust binary. It compiles, checks, serves and bundles npm packages by itself: no Vite, no esbuild, no config. You need a Rust toolchain (cargo, from rustup) to build it. Node 22 or newer is needed only when an app has .server.js files, because pragma dev, pragma serve and the Node adapter run them.

    git clone https://github.com/leonavas/pragma
cd pragma
cargo install --path core/cli/crates/pragma-cli
     
    pragma -V
pragma 0.1.0
pragma --help
pragma — HTML, CSS and JS without a framework

usage:
  pragma new <dir>                              create an app in <dir> (empty or missing)
  pragma dev [--port 5180] [--host 127.0.0.1]   dev server with live reload
  pragma build                                  build dist/ for production
  pragma check [--strict]                       check HTML, CSS and JS (--strict: warnings become errors)
  pragma serve [--port 3000] [--host 127.0.0.1] serve dist/ as in production
  pragma upgrade                                update .pragma/ (runtime, docs, base.css, version) to this version
  pragma self-update [version]                  update the pragma CLI binary from GitHub Releases

options:
  -h, --help      show this help
  -V, --version   show the version

    Options take either form, --port 8080 or --port=8080. The cargo install output and the clone progress are left out above.

    To update, run git pull and the same cargo install, then pragma upgrade inside each app. It makes the app's .pragma/ (runtime, docs, base.css) match the new binary, prints every file it updated, added or removed, and never touches anything outside .pragma/. Until then pragma check warns with app/core-outdated.

    Create an app

    pragma new writes a working app into an empty or missing folder: a layout, a home page with a modal, an alert and a dropdown, a 404 page, the theme, the runtime in .pragma/ and the docs in .pragma/docs/.

    pragma new my-app
app created in my-app (41 files)

  cd my-app
  pragma dev

    The app ships an AGENTS.md (and a CLAUDE.md that includes it) with the syntax in a dozen lines, the rules the compiler enforces and a table that maps each task to one file in .pragma/docs/. A coding agent reads that first; you can too. The docs are short on purpose: every page fits in a context window.

    Your first component

    A component is a folder with one .html file: an optional <script>, the markup, an optional <style>. In the script, a top-level let is state, a function is an action when an event calls it and a derived value when the markup reads it, and export let declares a prop. In the markup, {$count} puts a value in the text, @click calls a function and :disabled binds an attribute. Assigning a variable is all it takes to update the page.

    Use it on any page. The build expands it in place, so its markup is in the prebuilt HTML, and its script loads only on pages that use it: a page with just this counter loads 8.9 kB of JS, runtime included.

    <c-counter label="Cups of coffee" start="1"></c-counter>
    • The default sets the prop's type: start="1" arrives as the number 1 because the default is 0; a bare attribute is true.
    • Props are read-only and live. let count = start copies one into state that the component can change.
    • The <style> is scoped to the markup the component wrote; utilities from classes.md cover the rest.
    • pragma check reads the script: a name the markup uses but the script lacks is html/unknown-name, an attribute the component does not declare is html/unknown-prop, a write to a prop is js/prop-write.

    Project structure

    The layout is fixed, so there is nothing to configure and only one place for each thing. The files below are exactly what pragma new creates, minus .pragma/.

    pragma.json               name, lang and webmcp
AGENTS.md  CLAUDE.md      rules for coding agents
routes/
  _layout.html            header, footer, site-wide <head>; <slot> is the page
  _404.html               unknown URLs
  index.html              /         (markup, its <script> and <style>)
lib/
  components/<name>/      <c-name> for every page: modal, alert, dropdown
  state/<name>.js         stores, reached as shared.<name>
  theme.css               tokens and the few custom classes
utils/                    plain JS modules
public/                   copied as is: favicon.svg, images, fonts
.pragma/                  runtime and docs; never edited
    • Only routes/, lib/, utils/, .pragma/ and public/ are read. Other top-level files, like a README, are ignored.
    • A page is routes/x.html, with an optional <script> and <style> at its top level and an optional x.server.js (load, server actions, ssr). A large script can live in x.js beside it instead, never both (html/duplicate-module).
    • Anything else in routes/ must be private, with a leading underscore: _components/, _products.json, _catalog.server.js.
    • pragma.json takes exactly name (required: fallback title, log service name, Worker name), lang (default en) and webmcp (default true). Unknown keys are errors.

    Develop

    pragma dev builds into .pragma/dev/, watches the folder and reloads every open tab on each save, over one WebSocket per tab. CSS changes swap in place without a reload.     The rules form a closed list. Anything outside the syntax is an error with a pointer to the fix, so an agent cannot quietly drift into another framework's habits.

    • JS: js/syntax, js/comment, js/console, js/vague-name, js/html-in-js (no innerHTML or createElement), js/jsdoc-types, js/import, and the script rules: js/component-script (no var, no top-level await, export only for props), js/prop-write, js/const-state (a mutated const the markup reads), js/store-import (stores only through shared) and js/legacy-api (the old state(ctx) API, with the migration).
    • HTML: html/syntax (close every non-void tag), html/comment, html/script, html/duplicate-module (a <script> and an x.js for the same file), html/style-inline, html/on-inline, html/legacy-syntax, html/unknown-directive, html/invalid-path, html/invalid-root, the block rules (html/block, html/for-without-key, html/misplaced-else…), html/unknown-name, html/unknown-prop, html/component, html/unknown-component, html/layout, html/title, html/class (no :class), html/text-removed (no :text), html/interpolation (no {{ }} or ${ } outside <code>/<pre>), html/data-attribute (no hand-written data-*) and html/head (<meta> and <link> only at the top of a page or in the layout head). html/unknown-directive also names the pragma form for Vue, Alpine, Svelte, Angular and React attributes.
    • CSS: css/syntax, css/comment, css/unknown-class (only the utilities in classes.md and classes your CSS defines), css/arbitrary-value.
    • App: app/structure, app/route-conflict, app/package, app/pragma-json, and the warning app/core-outdated when .pragma/ differs from the installed binary.
    • Accessibility, checked on the expanded page with components inlined: img-alt, accessible-name, label, dialog-name, click-non-interactive, heading, single-h1, tabindex, duplicate-id, iframe-title, a-no-href. A bound attribute counts: :aria-label satisfies aria-label.

    Performance

    pragma build prints the JS each page loads, gzip, runtime included, and the CSS size. The numbers are information only: no limit fails the build.

    A page with no script of its own costs 8.7 kB gzip, all of it runtime. When a page grows, make the code smaller. What the build does to keep pages small:

    • Every route is prebuilt HTML, and a page with a load starts its data fetch from an inline script in <head>, before any module runs.
    • Exactly the modules a page imports get a modulepreload. Modules are minified and hashed one by one; there is no app bundle.
    • The bodies of <if> and <for> blocks go to one preloaded template module per page; the HTML keeps a short comment where each block renders.
    • The CSS contains only the classes the app uses.
    • Links prefetch on hover, focus or when visible; navigations use view transitions.
    • HTML is served no-cache, /assets/ as immutable, both brotli or gzip compressed. A file in public/ that the CSS names with url(/…) (a font, a background image) gets a hashed copy in /assets/, so a returning visit uses it from cache with no request.
    • Code needed only after a click goes behind await import() in the action: not preloaded, not in the page size. See lazy packages.

    Under the hood

    Nothing here needs configuring, but it helps when you read the built HTML or debug a deploy.

    • The generated <head> comes in this order: charset, viewport, <title>, the layout's head tags (a page's own <meta> and <link> replace the layout's tag with the same name), the theme script when used, the stylesheet, the inline /_data fetch when the page has a load, the modulepreloads, the route JSON and the boot module.
    • The route JSON, a <script> with id="pragma-route", tells the runtime what to start: 
      {"pattern":"/orders","page":null,"components":{},"stores":{},"loader":true,"ssr":false}
    • /_pragma/manifest.json lists every route with its HTML file, modules, loader and SSR flag. The client router and the Node adapter both read it.
    • Data travels as GET /_data/<path> and server actions as POST /_action/<path>/<name>, both with a traceparent header.
    • Not in v0: static generation with data, catch-all routes ([...rest]), per-route CSS, i18n and Speculation Rules.

The speed of one HTML file, built to scale

No framework beats plain HTML, CSS and JS in one file. It just doesn't scale.

pragma gives that code a structure that grows: routes, components, stores, one way to do each thing. The build keeps the speed: prebuilt HTML, no virtual DOM, one JS chunk per route and only the CSS each page can match.

Hand it to your agent

Nobody argues about frameworks anymore. The agent picks one.

Most people who build with an LLM don't know frontend. They ask for React or Angular because those are the names they know, and ship slow pages.

Some don't care and get plain HTML and JavaScript. Nothing beats it on speed. Nothing about it scales: it eats context, turns into a tangle, and the agent loses the thread.

Some know a bit more and pick SvelteKit, Astro or htmx. Good tools, made for people who read docs.

pragma is made for the agent:

  • The minimum lint that stops the tangle: one way to do each thing, and every error names the rule and the fix.
  • Components and reactivity on what the browser already has: ES modules, <template>, <dialog>, popover, view transitions.
  • One Rust binary compiles, lints and validates. No Vite, no config.
  • Plain JavaScript. Never TypeScript.
  • WebMCP by default: every form is a tool an agent in the browser can call. A page with a .md next to it answers in markdown when an agent asks.

One file: markup, script and style

A component is one .html file. A top-level let is state, a function is an action, and {path} puts a value in the text. Add a task: the action changes tasks and the runtime updates the list. No hooks, no virtual DOM. The form is also a WebMCP tool: an agent in the browser can call add_task.

Four constraints, enforced by the compiler

Native

A page or a component is one .html file: the markup, its <script> and its <style>. Its data comes from the .server.js with the same name. No JSX, no virtual DOM, no framework between you and the platform.

Closed

Braces put a value in text, a colon binds an attribute, a dot a class, an at sign an event, a dollar sign names the script's state. Conditions and loops are tags. Anything outside that list is a build error, not a convention.
